title: The Storm That Changed How I See the Sea
script: Narrator: [warmly] Last month, I rented a small wooden house near the coast, because I wanted a quiet week away from my noisy apartment in the city.
Narrator: On the third evening, the sky turned a strange greenish color, and the fishermen on the beach started pulling their boats up quickly.
Narrator: [concerned] I asked one of them what was happening, and he simply said, a storm is coming, go inside now and stay away from the windows.
Narrator: Within an hour, the wind grew so strong that the whole house creaked, and the waves crashed against the rocks like something alive and angry.
Narrator: [honestly] I was frightened, although I was safe inside, because I had never seen the sea behave with such raw, uncontrollable power before.
Narrator: I moved to an interior area away from the windows, checked official weather alerts, and kept a charged light and emergency bag nearby.
Narrator: [relieved] After an official update said the worst had passed around midnight, the wind calmed, and the rain softened into a gentle patter on the roof above my head.
Narrator: The next morning, I walked out to a completely different beach. The sand was smoother, and strange shells had washed up everywhere along the shore.
Narrator: [thoughtful] The same fisherman was already back near his boat, checking the ropes calmly, as if nothing unusual had happened the night before.
Narrator: I asked him if storms like that scared him after so many years of fishing this coast.
Narrator: [reflective] He smiled and said the sea gives generously most days, so he doesn't complain when it occasionally reminds everyone who is truly in control.
Narrator: His answer stayed with me long after I left that coast and returned to my ordinary city routine.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now, whenever I feel like I control everything in my life, I remember that greenish sky and those crashing waves.
Narrator: Nature does not need our permission to be powerful, and respecting it includes following safety warnings, and honestly, that thought makes me feel smaller in a good, humbling way.
